Three things happened for Ramp investors on the same day:
The good news:
Brex essentially acknowledged Ramp won, even if they aren’t 100% direct competitors in every segment and with every product today. Started later, doing $1 billion to Brex’s $700 million.
The uncomfortable news:
When real money—not a secondary buyer purchasing 2% of the cap table—wrote an actual check for the whole asset, they valued it at 7x revenue. If you multiply Ramp’s billion-dollar run rate by 7, you get $7 billion. Even doubling it for faster growth gets you to $15 billion. Ramp raised at $32 billion.
The structural news:
Capital One now owns both Discover (closed for $50 billion) and Brex. Discover has a closed network—meaning Cap One captures all the interchange instead of splitting it with Visa and Mastercard. They can now route Brex spend onto their own rails.
If you’re Ramp, you’re now playing against the A-team with a structural cost advantage.
The mark-to-market conversation is going to be awkward: How do you factor in a comparable transaction at 7x revenue when your last round implied 30x?

hubristic fundraising

Let me define it simply: Hubristic fundraising is when you raise at a valuation so aggressive, with terms so favorable, with a narrative so bold, that you are essentially betting the entire future of your company on hitting an extraordinary outcome. It’s not just “raising a lot of money.” Plenty of companies raise hundreds of millions without hubris. Hubristic fundraising is when you:
Take a valuation that requires Top 0.1%+ annual growth for a decade to grow into
Raise at 100x-500x+ revenue multiple. Often, again and again. Build your entire talent acquisition, press strategy, and customer pitch around being “the most valuable” or “fastest-growing”

These deals can work out.

Does Jason Lemkin say a great VP of Sales should immediately bring in more sales executives, or that criticizing a VP of Sales who cannot do better is counterproductive?
A great VP of Sales will generally bring in at least one or two top performers with them. But it’s rarely all the way up to half the team they bring in with them. More here:
How Your First Great VP of Sales Really Works — And When You Hire Them | SaaStr
And as part of that … you need to give her time. Time to make changes and grow the team under her. The best VPs of Sales are magicians. They know how to take your existing leads and customers and close even more. It can take some time, though. So I’m surprised when founders criticize their VPs of Sales for not closing more revenue faster than she did before. That just doesn’t work out well. More on that here:
What Happens If You Fire Your First VP Of Sales?

The VP of Sales needs to be at least as good as your VP of Marketing. “When you have to question if they’re working out.” — Team EPECC
Yup. This is so true. Even if you are no sales expert yourself, you should see enough improvements in sales in the first 30 days of a VP of Sales that you know it’s working. If you don’t think it is … it isn’t. More time does not solve this. A tough lesson so many founders have to learn. “Brought in sales consultants” — Rob Boyle
It might be OK for a VP of Sales to bring in a Salesforce consultant to help with Salesforce, or a little help on revenue operations, in the first 30 days. But too many agencies and consultants is a big flag. It’s a sign they don’t actually know how to do it themselves. “He would get so mad in sales team meetings his face would turn red.” — Josh Buttita
VP of Sales is a tough job. It requires passion and a challenging combination of urgency and patience. And the team always believing it can be done. And showing them it can be. “As head of product being told “if you can just keep up with me we’ll get to $100m ARR in no time” — Kevin O’Neill, VP Product, Splash
I like this challenge on some level :). But again, blaming product is a sign of a VP of Sales that won’t get there. Every startup is feature-poor and had feature gaps. Product and Eng owe Sales more features every quarter. But no product will ever be 100% feature-complete vs. the competition. A great VP of Sales knows how best to work around that, and at least close more deals than closed before they arrived.

Too many VPs of Sales don’t help out on webinars, on lead scoring, on following up on marketing’s work. Then … marketing starts to focus more narrowly on its own specific KPIs and goals.
—————————-
What 3 factors/skills must every VP of sales possess? Why? Jason:
There are different types of VP of Sales for different phases of B2B companies. But if we’re talking, say, broadly from $1m-$50 in ARR, there are three top skills. And directly selling his or herself isn’t one of the top 3, interestingly. Ability to Recruit a Large and Successful Team
. Because you’re going to need a team to sell. And recruiting great reps and making them successful is the #1 most important thing your VP Sales will do. And the great VP of Sales all know this. They all either have in their back pocket, and/or are constantly on the prowl for, the next 2-3 great reps because sales is a lead-driven but headcount-closed business. To hit their number, they know they need the heads. It becomes mathematically impossible without them. Hands-On Enough to Backfill Her/His Sales Team
. Until you are relatively big, while the VP Sales won’t be able to take most deals personally, he or she will have to spend a ton of time helping his/her sales team close deals. Working and closing key deals with them. Spotting issues before they blow up and seeing opportunities ahead of the horizon. In general, the VP of Sales should be making sure his/her 3 reports, then 10 reports, then 30 direct and indirect reports — work as effectively and efficiently as they can. Sales Tactics
.

traces.answer:
Who said that AI means everything in SaaS needs to be a personalized experience?
I did. And I was wrong — sort of. It’s more nuanced than that. Let me explain what I mean, and why this matters if you’re running an SaaS company today.
The Personalization Revolution: Why We Were Wrong About Everything Being Personalized
AI has unleashed unprecedented capabilities across every aspect of B2B software—customer support, marketing automation, sales engagement, product development, and operations. But here’s the thing:
the assumption that AI enables hyper-personalized experiences for every single touchpoint has been wildly oversold.
Yes, AI makes personalization easier and better than ever before. Yes, customers expect highly tailored interactions. Yes, AI can create remarkable one-to-one experiences at scale. But should we push ourselves to try harder to achieve them with AI? Is it worth the investment? Not always. In fact, many businesses have discovered that the ROI math just doesn’t justify full-on personalization for every interaction. Here’s why.
Why Hyper-Personalization Isn’t Always Worth It (And What This Means for Your Business)
Let’s look at some hard data:
Support tickets are still mostly solved with bots and AI
. Most customer service issues don’t require human empathy—they need quick resolution through well-trained AI agents. Marketing campaigns perform better when batched
. Segment-of-one messaging sounds great in theory, but research shows that grouping similar segments together often yields stronger results due to economies of scale. Automation beats personalization for routine tasks
. When customers want help renewing their subscription, updating billing information, or accessing account settings, they actually prefer streamlined automated processes over personalized chat sessions.

So who said that AI means everything in SaaS needs to be a personalized experience?
There’s one guy. That I know that did say this. He's right. But he’s also wrong. It was me.
I think we need two different types of experiences today in B2B and SaaS. We need one where you expect an AI to answer your questions instantly and give you answers that are better than any human ever could. And then we need another type of product where humans deeply understand what they’re doing.
The first thing is just to look back. What has been our top performing content for years? All these pieces were written by humans. They're great. There's nothing wrong with them. And yet, if we took those same topics and asked Claude to summarize them more concisely without the extra words, how much time would we save? And when I compare my last three weeks as CEO to being VP of Marketing before, I've already saved like four hours per day. This is just a fraction of what I could do.
But the point is, so many things that used to require a lot of human effort now seem to be able to be done very efficiently by AI. And there seems to be no end in sight. So let’s break it down into three buckets. First bucket—things humans don't really want to do anymore. Things that are repetitive, unrewarding, or don't scale. If you had to hire someone to go out and follow up with every single lead that came into your CRM versus having someone just qualify leads and pass them to sales, which would you rather do? You'd rather pay some human to do the unglamorous parts than actually get on planes and meet with customers and sell stuff.
And here’s the reality check—there probably aren’t enough humans to even do these jobs. We’ve already lost millions of workers in tech since Covid, folks leaving their job, etcetera.
